summary: Zacharias Frankel (1801-1875), born in Prague in Bohemia, was a rabbi and scholar who founded the 'positive-historical' school of Judaism (positiv-historisches Judentum), the intellectual forerunner of Conservative (Masorti) Judaism. Affirming the historical-critical study of the Jewish sources (Wissenschaft des Judentums), he nonetheless broke with the radical Reform of his day, notably over the centrality of the Hebrew language and the binding force of halakha, seceding from the 1845 Frankfurt rabbinical conference when it moved to set Hebrew aside in worship. From 1854 he directed the newly founded Jewish Theological Seminary of Breslau, the first modern rabbinical seminary in Central Europe, which combined critical scholarship with traditional observance. His 'positive-historical' approach is described here as his own attributed position.
description:
Zacharias Frankel, born in Prague in 1801, trained in both traditional Talmudic learning and the university studies then newly open to Jews in Central Europe, and served as a rabbi (in Bohemia and later as chief rabbi in Dresden) before becoming the founding director of the Breslau seminary. He is remembered in the scholarship as the founder of what he called positiv-historisches Judentum, the 'positive-historical' school, which the historians of the later movement (Michael A. Meyer, Moshe Davis, Ismar Schorsch) identify as the intellectual forerunner of Conservative (Masorti) Judaism. He died in Breslau in 1875.

The 'positive-historical' approach, presented here as Frankel's own attributed position, combined two commitments that he held together. It was 'historical' in that it acknowledged that Judaism has a history and did not descend ready-made from heaven, and so submitted the Jewish past, including the classical sources, to free scholarly inquiry, the Wissenschaft des Judentums (the 'science of Judaism'); Frankel's own scholarship, in works on the Septuagint, on the Mishnah (his Darkhei ha-Mishnah), and on the development of Jewish law, was an exercise of exactly this historical-critical method. It was 'positive' in that it held fast, at the same time, to the practical observance of the commandments and to the received forms of the tradition as the tradition has come to embody them, so that critical scholarship was not to dissolve observance but to accompany it. On this account the authority of Jewish practice rests less on a moment-by-moment appeal to revelation than on the historical continuity and the will of the community of Israel as a whole (Klal Yisrael), a theme later drawn out by his successors.

Frankel's break with radical Reform is the episode by which his position is most often defined. In the German rabbinical conferences of the 1840s, convened to reform Jewish worship and law, Frankel took part but came into conflict with the more radical reformers. At the Frankfurt conference of 1845, when the assembly moved to treat the Hebrew language as no longer essential to public worship and to permit its wide replacement by the vernacular, Frankel seceded, holding the centrality of Hebrew and, more broadly, the binding character of the received tradition and halakha to be non-negotiable. In the scholarship (Meyer, Response to Modernity) this secession is read as a defining moment: Frankel affirmed historical-critical scholarship as fully as the reformers did, but refused their conclusion that the community might set aside traditional observance in the light of reason, and so charted a distinct middle path. From 1854 he directed the newly founded Jewish Theological Seminary (Jüdisch-Theologisches Seminar) of Breslau, the first modern rabbinical seminary in Central Europe, which trained a generation of rabbis and scholars in the union of Wissenschaft with traditional piety and is regarded as the academic precursor of the later Conservative movement.

Where the positive-historical school and its heirs differ from the Orthodox and Reform movements over the authority and mutability of halakha and over the scope of historical criticism, those differences are stated on each movement's own terms in the conservative-judaism, orthodox-judaism, and reform-judaism entries. This entry describes Frankel and his positive-historical position, and does not rule which movement's account of Judaism is the authentic or correct one.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Zacharias Frankel as the founder of the 'positive-historical' school (positiv-historisches Judentum), given throughout as HIS OWN ATTRIBUTED position, described and not affirmed or denied by the editor (neutrality #1, #4): the twin commitments, 'historical' (free historical-critical inquiry, Wissenschaft des Judentums) and 'positive' (fidelity to the observance of the commandments and the received tradition), are stated as Frankel's own combination, and his 1845 Frankfurt secession over the centrality of Hebrew and the binding force of halakha as historical event and as his stated conviction. The intra-Jewish denominational crux, which movement is the authentic or correct Judaism, is NOT adjudicated: the differences among the positive-historical / Conservative, Orthodox, and Reform positions are stated on each movement's own terms and deferred to the respective entries (neutrality #1-#2), mirroring the existing conservative-judaism and reform-judaism entries' handling. Sources triangulate three lenses per neutrality #8-9: (a) academic historians, Michael A. Meyer, Response to Modernity (the standard history of the Reform movement, which treats Frankel's positive-historical secession in detail), and Moshe Davis, The Emergence of Conservative Judaism (the standard history of the historical school); (b) the tradition's own voice via a contemporary Jewish scholar within the movement, Ismar Schorsch, whose work on Frankel and the European origins of Conservative Judaism carries the movement's account of its founder; (c) the programmatic Frankel primary is noted but NOT relied on as an open read (see below). No encyclopedias (no Encyclopaedia Judaica, no Jewish Encyclopedia, no Britannica, no My Jewish Learning), no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. CONFIDENCE / HONESTY: this entry tops out at REVIEWED and its sources at MEDIUM. Frankel's programmatic statements of positive-historical Judaism (his prospectus for the Zeitschrift für die religiösen Interessen des Judenthums, his 1845 conference statements, Darkhei ha-Mishnah) survive largely in nineteenth-century German and Hebrew scholarly editions that are NOT openly readable in reliable English online, so NO open primary was read line-by-line for this figure and NONE is invented; the positive-historical position is carried here through the secondary scholarship (Meyer, Davis, Schorsch), which is verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher, library, and review records but not read line-by-line, hence medium. Unlike solomon-schechter, whose Studies in Judaism is public domain and was read line-by-line (high), Frankel has no equivalent open English primary, so this entry is honestly reviewed-only. sources.citation: Meyer, Michael A. Response to Modernity: A History of the Reform Movement in Judaism. Studies in Jewish History. New York: Oxford University Press, 1988 (reprinted Detroit: Wayne State University Press, 1995). The standard scholarly history of the Reform movement, which treats Zacharias Frankel and the emergence of the positive-historical school in detail, including his participation in and secession from the German rabbinical conferences of the 1840s (notably the 1845 Frankfurt conference over the Hebrew language) and his direction of the Breslau seminary; cited as the academic-historian lens on Frankel's positive-historical position and its break with radical Reform. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Oxford University Press / Wayne State University Press record; reviewed in AJS Review and the American Historical Review), not read line-by-line.

Davis, Moshe. The Emergence of Conservative Judaism: The Historical School in 19th Century America. Philadelphia: The Jewish Publication Society of America, 1963. The standard scholarly history of the 'historical school', tracing the movement whose intellectual antecedent is Frankel's positive-historical Judaism; cited as an academic-historian lens on the school Frankel founded and its later development. Verified to exist and be on-topic (JPS, 1963; WorldCat record confirms author, title, subtitle, publisher, and year), not read line-by-line.
